Q: How to efficiently query and paginate across multiple tenant-specific MongoDB databases in a multi-tenant SaaS? A:

Go with Option 3 (summary collection) — it's the standard pattern here. Use Change Streams on each tenant DB to auto-sync into public_properties (more reliable than updating from API code, since it catches all writes). Store only the fields needed for filtering/sorting (tenant_id, createdAt, forSale, forRental, etc.), index {forSale, forRental, createdAt}, and fetch full details from the tenant DB only when needed.

$unionWith won't work since it can't dynamically span multiple databases, and backend-side looping won't scale or paginate correctly once you have many tenants.

Q: looking for embedded webrtc solution for ip camera? A:

go2rtc/Janus/mediasoup are all solid picks for the gateway layer, as mentioned above. A couple of things worth adding for the specific constraints you listed:

For sub-200ms glass-to-glass with two-way audio, the biggest latency source usually isn't the gateway, it's transcoding. If the camera can already produce a WebRTC-friendly H.264 profile (baseline/main, short keyframe interval), pick a gateway that passes it through instead of re-encoding — go2rtc and mediasoup can both do this. Re-encoding on a low-end camera-side box will blow past 200ms almost immediately.

For native + Flutter, plan for your own signaling layer (WebSocket/Socket.io) regardless of which gateway you choose — the browser-embed endpoints (e.g. go2rtc's WHEP/WHIP) don't cover mobile SDK negotiation by themselves. If a minimal working example is more useful than assembling one from the gateway docs, VideoWhisper's videowhisper-webrtc (https://github.com/videowhisper/videowhisper-webrtc) is a small open-source Node.js signaling server, paired with a React reference app (github.com/videowhisper/Webcam-Streaming-WebRTC) that does camera-to-browser WebRTC with two-way audio end to end.

On "P2P": true mesh P2P only really holds up for 1 camera to 1 viewer. Once you add a second viewer, or need a relay for NAT traversal (likely on real-world networks), you're effectively running an SFU no matter what it's branded as — so I'd choose based on TURN/STUN and mobile SDK support rather than the P2P label.

Q: Maven build errors for Java app referencing org.controlsfx A:

Preface: This answer is incomplete. It explains what's going wrong and how it doesn't appear to be your fault. But a full solution is not offered because I don't know NetBeans, which I assume is the culprit, well enough.

Your code and POM file are correct. The following command executes without errors for me:

mvn process-classes exec:exec

Note: That runs the process-classes lifecycle and then runs the org.codehaus.mojo:exec-maven-plugin:exec goal.

However, that's not the command you're executing. You have:

/snap/netbeans/145/netbeans/java/maven/bin/mvn \
    -Dexec.vmArgs= \
    "-Dexec.args=${exec.vmArgs} -classpath %classpath ${exec.mainClass} ${exec.appArgs}" \
    -Dexec.appArgs= \
    -Dexec.mainClass=com.example.App \
    -Dexec.executable=/data/stuart/Apps/zulu25.32.21-ca-fx-jdk25.0.2-linux_x64/bin/java \
    --no-transfer-progress \
    process-classes \
    org.codehaus.mojo:exec-maven-plugin:3.5.1:exec

Note: Those ${<key>} parts are substituted (by Maven) with the value of the <key> property.

I assume this command is not actually being executed by you, but rather by NetBeans. Regardless, if you look at that command you can see it sets various system properties, including exec.args. That property can be used to override the <arguments> configuration in the POM file.

In your POM you have:

<arguments>
  <arg>--module-path</arg>
  <modulepath/>
  <arg>--enable-native-access=javafx.graphics</arg>
  <arg>--add-exports</arg>
  <arg>javafx.base/com.sun.javafx.event=org.controlsfx.controls</arg>
  <arg>--add-exports</arg>
  <arg>javafx.controls/com.sun.javafx.scene.control.behavior=org.controlsfx.controls</arg>
  <arg>--module</arg>
  <arg>app/com.example.App</arg>
</arguments>

Which is properly setting up the module-path and launching your application as a modular application. But the command you're executing overrides all that by setting the exec.args property:

"-Dexec.args=${exec.vmArgs} -classpath %classpath ${exec.mainClass} ${exec.appArgs}"

Now everything is being placed on the class-path and your application is being launched as a non-modular application. Hence the error you're getting:

Error: JavaFX runtime components are missing, and are required to run this application

Which occurs when the main class is a subtype of javafx.application.Application but the javafx.graphics module is not present in the boot module layer. In other words, the javafx.graphics module was not loaded as a named module from the --module-path but was instead loaded into the unnamed module from the --class-path. An unsupported workaround for this is to have a separate "launcher" main class that simply launches the JavaFX framework, but in your case the proper solution is to fix the command you're using to execute the application.

Additionally, be aware that the command you're executing no longer passes the --add-exports options. Meaning if it weren't for the above error you'd be getting the same error(s) you were getting in your previous question.

Unfortunately, I have not used NetBeans in a long time nor do I have it installed, so I don't know what you need to do to get it to execute the exec-maven-plugin:exec goal correctly. I would look for a way to execute Maven lifcycles/goals directly.

Q: Wrong manual caching of recursion A:

Given 𝑛=68, the challenge asks how many distinct values there are for the expression 3𝑘−2𝑚 where 𝑘+𝑚=𝑛 and 𝑘, 𝑚 are non-negative integers.

So for a given 𝑛 and a given 𝑘, the value is 3𝑘−2(𝑛−𝑘), i.e. 5𝑘−2𝑛

As 𝑘, 𝑚 are non-negative integers, the possible values for 𝑘 are in {0, 1, 2, ..., 𝑛}, and so we have 𝑛+1 distinct values of the form 5𝑘−2𝑛. It should be clear these are distinct, as the term −2𝑛 is constant for a given 𝑛: in sorted order two consecutive values differ by 5.

In short, no program is needed. The answer is 𝑛+1. For the case of 68, the answer is 69.

Q: Is there a way to style Google Chrome default PDF viewer A:

For people years later looking for how to control the PDF background color beside the pages in Chromium-based browsers, it's technically possible with another method.

I have created PDF Dark Overlay for Chrome PDF Viewer for this. This uses Tampermonkey (although you can do it temporarily on the page); for easy repetition the next time you want to activate a clean dark mode together with the background.

Adds sidebar masks and backdrop-filter over Chrome's PDF viewer, allowing tools like Dark Reader to have a clean dark PDF viewer without:

  1. recompiling and changing the background color every update,

  2. filtering only all colors unselectively,

  3. page resizing until the background disappears,

  4. transferring to a different PDF viewer, often requiring uploads for every file you look at, unlike the built-in Chrome viewer.

Drag the overlay edges to resize them or use the floating menu to adjust brightness and offset.

Tweaks automatically save per user, and defaults can be changed in the variables section.

Requires Allow access to file URLs to reach file:/// or objects in files, as well as the Allow User Scripts so that Tampermonkey can run.

USERSCRIPT LINK (get the Tampermonkey Chrome extension if you do not have it and add the requirements to run on files):

https://greasyfork.org/en/scripts/588718-pdf-native-viewer-dark-overlay

GITHUB (if you want to see the code or full description): https://github.com/Artectdis/pdf-dark-overlay

Q: Use git to list differences with their respective line blame information A:

This isn't a common enough workflow that anybody's built it as a convenience command or option, seems pretty straightforward to implement though: diff the blamed versions.

git diff --name-only this that \
| while read f
  do git diff --no-index <(git blame this -- "$f") <(git blame that -- "$f")
  done

with whatever other pretties you care to implement.
